summary.text:
Harrow publishes a treasury contact with an address, so it is email-ready, and the report has an unusual amount that ties. Our PWLB file holds 19 loans at £408,461,000 and a weighted 3.5685% against their Table 8 PWLB row of £408,461k at 3.57% — to the pound and to the basis point. Table 8 foots and reblends completely, including the 27.27-year average life. The balance sheet identity closes exactly: CFR £597,459k less £455,674k of borrowing less £23,996k of lease liabilities is the £117,789k of under-borrowing they print.

The lead is paragraph 8.4. Harrow's final LOBO counterparty exercised its option to raise the rate; the council declined; the £20.8m was repaid. That is the eleventh LOBO call in our file and the largest single one, and as with the ten before it the borrower refused. Harrow is now LOBO-free. The arithmetic ties to the thousand pounds — the £22.104m fall in market loans in Table 8 is the £20.8m LOBO plus the £1.304m of other repayments named in the same paragraph — and the £65m of PWLB drawn to fund it is exactly the movement in the PWLB row.

Second, the West London Waste Authority loan: £15m advanced in July 2013 for 25 years at 7.604%, £13.9m still outstanding, £1.074m of income in the year. That is the highest sustained inter-authority rate in our whole file — Cornwall's 8.50% was for four days, this has about ten years to run — and it was budgeted to supply 42% of the year's investment income.

Third, Table 10 reprints the November 2024 forecast that paragraph 8.5 says drove the duration of the new borrowing. Scored at March 2026 it was right on Bank Rate (3.75% forecast, 3.75% actual, as 8.9 says) and 100 to 120 basis points below the PWLB curve that actually arrived. On today's repayment curve the book carries about £104.2m of net discount, £93.5m of it in four long loans.

Balance sheet: CFR £597,459k − £455,674k − £23,996k = £117,789k, the printed under-borrowing; and 455,674 + 23,996 = 479,670 gross debt. Tables 1 and 2 foot in every column. §8.11: 1.580 + 1.163 = 2.743 and 2.743 − 2.420 = 0.323; §11.2: 3.615 − 0.323 = 3.292. officer.body:
Hi Patrick,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to GARMS on 9 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 19 PWLB loans for Harrow totalling £408,461,000 at a weighted 3.5685%, against the £408,461k at 3.57% in your Table 8 — to the pound and to the basis point. The rest of Table 8 reblends too, including the 27.27-year average life, which is not something we can usually reproduce. And the balance sheet closes exactly: CFR £597,459k less £455,674k of borrowing less £23,996k of lease liabilities is the £117,789k of under-borrowing in Table 4.

We wrote because of paragraph 8.4.

Your final LOBO counterparty triggered its option, asked for a higher rate, you declined, and the £20.8m was repaid. We have been tracking LOBO calls across the sector since the spring, and yours is the eleventh we have picked up — across eight councils now — and the largest single one. What is striking is that all eleven went the same way: in every case the borrower declined the new rate and the loan was repaid or refinanced. Not one authority in our file has accepted an increase.

That matters more than it looks. The instrument is written so the lender's option only pays if the borrower accepts, and a sector-wide refusal rate of eleven out of eleven says the option is worth very little at current rates — which is presumably why your counterparty exercised at all, and why the outcome was the one you chose. We publish that pattern because no single council can see it from its own book. Dexia is on the other side of six of the LOBO books we hold; yours is now closed.

The arithmetic in the same paragraph is worth noting, because it is unusually clean. The £22.104m fall in market loans in Table 8 is exactly your £20.8m LOBO plus the £1.304m of other principal repayments you name. And the £65m of PWLB in 8.5 is exactly the movement in the PWLB row, £343,461k to £408,461k. A reader can verify the whole transaction from two paragraphs and one table.

Second, the West London Waste Authority loan. £15m advanced in July 2013 for twenty-five years at 7.604%, £13.9m outstanding, £1.074m earned in the year. Of everything we have read this year that is the highest sustained inter-authority rate anywhere by a wide margin. The headline numbers in this market are short — Cornwall paid 8.50% for four days over the year end, Harlow 7.75% for a month, Bexley 7.00% for 32 days — and none of them lasts. Yours has about ten years still to run. It is also, on your own 8.11, 42% of the year's investment income budget from one counterparty, which is the sort of concentration that is invisible in a portfolio table because the loan sits outside it.

Third, and this one is offered as an observation rather than anything more. Table 10 is one of very few forecast tables we see reprinted in a form that can be scored after the fact, and your 8.5 says the short duration of the new £65m was chosen on the strength of forecasts expecting further rate reductions. Scored at March 2026: the Bank Rate line was right, 3.75% forecast and 3.75% delivered, which your 8.9 rightly points out. The PWLB lines were 100 to 120 basis points below what arrived — 4.70% forecast against a 5.72% ten-year certainty rate, 5.10% against 6.29% at twenty-five years, 4.90% against 6.08% at fifty. Both calls came from the same table, and the one that was right is the one that governs reinvestment while the one that was wrong governs the cost of the refinancing. We track the forecast-versus-outturn gap across advisers precisely because that asymmetry is easy to miss; today's actual curve is at pwlbtoday.org and the path we model is at pwlbtoday.org/predictor.

On the book itself: on the DMO's repayment curve this afternoon, 12 of your 19 loans price below par for about £104.4m of discount against £0.28m of premium on the other seven. Four loans carry £93.5m of that — the £88.461m at 3.48% to 2062, the two £50m loans at 2.20% and 2.31% to 2069, and the £30m at 2.75% to 2060. We're not suggesting anything follows: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Harrow. Alternatives to PWLB covers LOBOs and what the sector's call record now looks like. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to the WLWA loan. Reading the PWLBpredict goes to Table 10. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Annual Outturn Report 2025/26, Governance, Audit, Risk Management and Standards Committee, 9 July 2026. Appendix 1 is exempt and was not read.
